name: Ivory Brown
lede: Ivory Brown is a dark, yellowish brown named for ivory, and it is the single most common named color in our painting archive.

sections.title: Ivory at its darkest
sections.body:
The library records Ivory Brown from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, plate 8 C 12, first recorded about 1804 [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[autumn]], [[cafe-noir]], [[musk]] and [[japanese-bush-warbler-brown]], at 2.8, 3.2, 
In LCH terms it measures lightness 28, chroma 19, hue 75 degrees, the ISCC-NBS "dark yellowish brown" block, Munsell 0.8Y 2.7/3.1, between brown and [[yellow]] [1]. 8, 3.2, 3.8 and 4.3 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this color in 7,673 of 23,781 paintings, 32.27 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 5,767 [2]. That makes it more common than every other named color we track [2]. It peaks in the 1600s, at 32.6 percent of that century's 6,394 paintings, 1.4 times the expected rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often sits as a mid-tone, in 38 percent of its appearances [2].

Juan de Valdés Leal is its most devoted painter, carrying it in 11 of his 16 works here, 2.5 times the baseline [2]. The earliest match is dated 799; that is 1,131 years before the name's own first record, in 1930, so the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not evidence of the actual paint, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
